manual.brief: Field manual // cipher theory and field algorithms
manual.inGame.title: Cipher reference
manual.frequency.theory: Frequency analysis breaks monoalphabetic substitution: every alphabet letter is replaced by the same different letter throughout the message. Such a cipher preserves the statistics of the language, so the most common ciphertext letter most likely corresponds to the most common letter of the language.
manual.frequency.math: P(letter in plaintext) ≈ the letter's frequency in the language: "e" ≈ 12% in English, "o" ≈ 9–10% in Ukrainian. A ciphertext letter appears exactly as often as its preimage, so aligning the two histograms produces the first substitution hypotheses.
manual.frequency.step.1: Open the text-frequencies tab and compare it with the reference language histogram.
manual.frequency.step.2: Start with the most frequent letters and the shortest words.
manual.frequency.step.3: Form hypotheses: click a ciphertext letter and type the expected plaintext letter.
manual.frequency.step.4: Lock in confident mappings; keep the rest as drafts.
manual.frequency.step.5: Hunt for typical word endings and common letter pairs to close the decryption.
manual.caesar.theory: The Caesar cipher is the classic shift cipher: every plaintext letter is replaced by the letter a fixed number of positions further down the alphabet. Named after Gaius Julius Caesar, who used a shift of 3 for military correspondence.
manual.caesar.math: Encryption: C = (P + K) mod N; decryption: P = (C − K) mod N, where N is the alphabet length. In ShiftCrack the shift always lies between 4 and 15, so a manual search is feasible but never instant.
manual.caesar.step.1: Count how often every ciphertext letter appears.
manual.caesar.step.2: Find the most frequent letter — in English it is usually "e".
manual.caesar.step.3: Align the tallest ciphertext bar with the language's most frequent letter.
manual.caesar.step.4: Rotate the wheel until the words become readable.
manual.caesar.step.5: Verify the guess on a short word, then submit the report.
manual.vigenere.theory: The Vigenère cipher is polyalphabetic: every letter is shifted by the value of a repeating key letter. The same plaintext letter can turn into different ciphertext letters, so plain frequency analysis fails — the key length must be found first.
manual.vigenere.math: C_i = (P_i + K_{i mod m}) mod N, where m is the key length and N the alphabet size. Kasiski's method: a repeated n-gram appears when the same letters land on the same key position, so the distances between repetitions are multiples of m — their GCD reveals the key length.
manual.vigenere.step.1: Find repeated trigrams in the ciphertext (Kasiski tab).
manual.vigenere.step.2: Compute the distances between repetitions and their GCD — that is the key length.
manual.vigenere.step.3: Split the text into columns by key position.
manual.vigenere.step.4: Each column is its own Caesar cipher: crack the shifts with frequency analysis.
manual.vigenere.step.5: Assemble the key and verify the decryption.
manual.transposition.theory: A route transposition does not substitute letters — it moves them around. The text is written into a grid along a chosen route and read out row by row. Letter frequencies stay untouched, so frequency analysis is powerless: the geometry of the grid is the key.
manual.transposition.math: The ciphertext is a solid rectangular stream of cols × rows letters. The column count is a divisor of the ciphertext length: L = cols × rows, so cols is one of the divisors of L. Every route is a continuous path that visits each cell exactly once.
manual.transposition.step.1: Count the ciphertext length and list its divisors — each is a column-count candidate.
manual.transposition.step.2: Drag the grid corner until it becomes a perfect rectangle.
manual.transposition.step.3: Try the routes: row snake, column snake, spiral.
manual.transposition.step.4: Trace a path through the cells to assemble the text.
manual.transposition.step.5: Once the sentence forms, lock in the answer.
